title: Courtney Stodden Calls Out Seinfeld Star Jason Alexander Over Sexualized 2012 Sketch When She Was a Minor
excerpt: Stodden, who was 17 at the time, described being groped with a cellphone and told to return 'when you're 18' during a Funny or Die skit with Alexander.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Courtney Stodden criticized Jason Alexander for a sexualized sketch when she was 17.
  • The sketch featured Alexander groping Stodden while joking about her age.
  • Stodden's accusations highlight a pattern of exploitation by media figures during her youth.
  • Alexander has not publicly responded to Stodden's allegations regarding the sketch.
  • Stodden's revelations have sparked a broader conversation about the treatment of young women in entertainment.

Public Responses from Alexander
  • Courtney Stodden has publicly called out Jason Alexander for a 2012 Funny or Die sketch in which she appeared in a bikini at age 17 while Alexander used a cellphone to touch her breasts on camera.
  • Stodden described the experience as being treated as "a giant, sexual joke," with the crew laughing while Alexander's character told her to come back "when you're 18."
  • The accusation is part of Stodden's broader reckoning with celebrities and media figures who exploited or mistreated her during her teenage years in the public eye.
  • Alexander, best known for playing George Costanza on Seinfeld, has not publicly addressed Stodden's account of the sketch.

The Sketch That Crossed a Line

Courtney Stodden has renewed her public criticism of Jason Alexander, the actor best known for playing George Costanza on Seinfeld, over a 2012 Funny or Die sketch that she says crossed clear boundaries with a minor.

https://x.com/OKMagazine/status/2079357602828284347

The sketch in question, an episode of Alexander's comedy web series The Donny Clay Show, featured a 17-year-old Stodden appearing in a bikini alongside her then-husband, 51-year-old actor Doug Hutchison. Alexander, playing a satirical life coach character, used a cellphone to rub against Stodden's breasts on camera. His character then turned to the camera and told her to "come back on the show when you're 18, and I can have my way with you behind this couch," according to Stodden's account and contemporaneous reports from BuzzFeed and Perez Hilton.

> **"Chrissy Teigen sent her private direct messages telling her to "kill myself," Stodden alleged in 2021, in addition to public tweets mocking the teenager."**

"I was this joke. A giant, sexual joke. And looking back on all of this stuff, nobody wants to say anything about it. Apparently, it's OK to treat minors this way."

— Courtney Stodden, in an interview with The Daily Beast

A Pattern of Exploitation

Alexander is far from the only public figure Stodden has called out. In recent months, she has confronted a growing list of celebrities and media personalities who she says exploited or mistreated her while she was underage. Dr. Drew Pinsky conducted a breast ultrasound on Stodden during an episode of his show Lifechangers when she was 16, broadcast to a live studio audience. Chrissy Teigen sent her private direct messages telling her to "kill myself," Stodden alleged in 2021, in addition to public tweets mocking the teenager. Joy Behar called her a "slut" on air, and Courtney Love called her a "whore," according to Stodden.

Stodden first shot to public attention in 2011 at the age of 16 when she married Hutchison, then 51, with her parents' consent. What followed was years of tabloid coverage and public ridicule directed at the teenager rather than at the adult who had married her. Stodden has since described the relationship as grooming and abuse, and the couple's divorce was finalized in 2020.

![George Costanza. Alexander, best known for playing George Costanza on Seinfeld, has not publicly addressed Stodden's account of the sketch.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/7/70/George_Costanza.jpg)

The Broader Reckoning

A Pattern of Exploitation
›Dr. Drew conducted a breast ultrasound on Stodden at age 16.
›Chrissy Teigen sent Stodden messages urging self-harm.
›Joy Behar and Courtney Love publicly mocked Stodden.
›Stodden's marriage at 16 was seen as grooming and abuse.

Stodden's willingness to name names has reignited a conversation about how the entertainment industry and media treated young women in the 2010s. At the time, much of the sketch's content was brushed off as comedy. "So I gotta ask… Funny, Die or just creepy?" wrote one entertainment blog in 2012 after the sketch aired. Even outlets that noted the discomfort treated it as part of Stodden's existing tabloid persona rather than as a potential exploitation of a minor.

The cultural context has shifted considerably since then. The #MeToo movement, combined with renewed scrutiny of how the entertainment industry treated young women from Britney Spears to the former child stars of Nickelodeon, has made audiences far less willing to excuse behavior that sexualizes minors under the guise of satire.

Stodden, now 31 and married to film director Jared Safier since December 2024, has recently also revealed that she was diagnosed with Tourette Syndrome as an adult. The diagnosis, she said, explained the involuntary tics that were widely mocked during her early television appearances as a teenager, which many viewers assumed were signs of intoxication or deliberate provocative behavior.

What Comes Next

Cultural Shift in Accountability
›The #MeToo movement has changed perceptions of exploitation.
›Sketches once seen as comedy are now scrutinized.
›Stodden's story prompts reassessment of media treatment.
›Stodden diagnosed with Tourette Syndrome, previously mocked.

Alexander, who is 66 and continues to work in entertainment through voice acting roles and stage appearances, has not publicly responded to Stodden's account of the 2012 sketch. Neither has Funny or Die, which produced and hosted the video.

Whether Stodden's continued public pressure leads to any formal acknowledgment or apology remains to be seen. But the sustained attention to her story has already forced a reassessment of how a generation of media figures and entertainers treated a teenager in the spotlight — and what accountability, if any, should follow more than a decade later.
